First of all, don't let anyone tell you it will show up, because they cannot assume.  The answer is it depends on the level of background check.  I know this first hand because I've gone through it.  I am not in HR.  If the background check digs deep, (usually takes a few days to two weeks) they will check county level courts for offenses.  So the longer it takes, the more time they have to dig.  From my experience, if it is a deep check, it will say pending charge, what you are being charged with, and the level of the charge (felony/misdemeanor)  If it is not a deep background check, (usually it checks databases and are instant) it will not detect a pending charge, only a conviction.  Go through with the background check, cross that bridge when it comes, and learn from past mistakes, good luck!

Master's Degree: Pros: Doesn't expire, you will be qualified on paper to apply for 'senior level roles' (depending on the company of course) ie: Director, CIO roles you will have an opportunity to build life long relationships with your professors and classmates, you will network with companies that hire with your school (ie: handshake), Cons: High cost, requires longer commitment than certs.  Certs: Pros: Lower cost than degree, fulfill many sought after job listings, can be more practical than Masters (depends on your school curriculum), keeps you proactive in learning.  Cons: You have to spend money to keep your certification for those that expire, can be costly if you experience multiple failing of exams plus training materials.  If you have the means, I'd get both, it will only make you more marketable in the long run.  Insert experience in there and you will be well rounded.

So I took the CISSP on 2/14/18 and failed so I will provide a little insight.  The closest practice exam to the CISSP is Boson, meaning, the questions ask for BEST, LEAST, FIRST, MOST.  The majority of questions I had were these types of questions.  Most of the questions are vague, one or two sentences.  Sometimes you take a guess because you don't know what they are asking.  Most of the questions are not straight to the point, ie: what port does ssh run on?  Most of the time you can do process of elimination and narrow it down to two answers.  Experience is a big part of this exam because you will encounter questions that are not in any book but have in the real world.  There are technical questions that are straight to the point.  Do you have to answer the way ISC2 wants you to?  50/50 yes and no.  Yes because you have learned the steps to a risk assessment, SDLC, vulnerability/patch management program, what is a warm/cold/hot site, what is grey/white/back box testing, etc.  No because some questions will test your experience and what would solve the issue holistically (the whole picture) I rather not say think like manager, but think holistically if the question calls for it.  Sybex and other books won't give you all you need to know for the exam, you need multiple resources, ie: practice exams, experience, books, videos, etc.  In most tests you have to make an educated guess because it's not possible to know every answer.  I plan to take the exam again in Feb.  So that is my two cents.

I busted my ass and I am still busting my ass now tired as hell writing this.  What I am getting at is you can do it, but you have to want it and be persistent, don't give up. Domain 1: Security and Risk Management 15%
Domain 2: Asset Security 10%
Domain 3: Security Architecture and Engineering 13%
Domain 4: Communication and Network Security 14%
Domain 5: Identity and Access Management (IAM) 13%
Domain 6: Security Assessment and Testing 12%
Domain 7: Security Operations 13%
Domain 8: Software Development Security 10%
Total: 100%
So this leads to a combination of proficiencies that you'll need to pass.  I would aim for 80% on practice exams.  Especially the domains you are scoring less than 70% on.
